opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Jesus is speaking to the disciples after they begin arguing about who is greater. As conversations sometimes do, it drifts toward questions of importance — who stands higher, who holds the greater place.

“You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and the great ones make their authority over them felt. But it shall not be so among you. Rather, whoever wishes to be great among you shall be your servant; whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave. Just so, the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”
 — Matthew 20:25–28

Jesus is pointing to a contrast between two completely different ways power operates. The first is the one the world understands well. Authority flows downward. Status is displayed and enforced. Leadership means being served. Power protects position. He is not criticizing Gentiles as a people; He is simply describing how human systems tend to operate everywhere.
But then He reveals the order of the Kingdom. Authority still moves downward, but through service. Greatness is measured by who carries the weight of others. Leadership becomes responsibility for another’s good. Power becomes self-giving.
In the ancient world, great men had servants. Jesus says great men become servants. The word He uses is diakonos — one who attends to the needs of others. From this word, the Church later received the word deacon. Even in the language itself, the hierarchy quietly flips.
The worldly kingdom moves toward authority as control, status as privilege, and greatness as being served. The Kingdom shows authority as responsibility, status as sacrifice, and greatness as serving.
What Jesus is really doing here is redefining what holiness looks like in daily life. Greatness in the Kingdom often appears in simple things: carrying the heavier load, restraining the ego, protecting the vulnerable, choosing service when you could demand position. The shape of love becomes the shape of leadership.

The disciples will soon watch this unfold in the final week of His life. On Palm Sunday the crowds treat Him like a king. On Holy Thursday He kneels and washes their feet. On Good Friday He gives His life.

In the Roman world, a throne symbolized visible power, domination, and victory. Yet Jesus is revealed as King through His crucifixion.
The throne becomes a cross.

A crown is placed on His head. A robe is placed upon Him. A title is posted above Him. People bow in savage mockery. And in that moment, the mock coronation becomes the true coronation.

Now aren’t you glad you follow the true King?

So many of our fellow human beings are caught in another pursuit — climbing for position, recognition, the promise of getting ahead. And in the climb we begin to overlook one another. A brother. A mother. A colleague. People move past one another, sometimes even over one another, all for the sake of advancement.

And in the process, we lose one another.
Because the pursuit never satisfies. It always asks for more… and more… and more.
Maybe the place to begin is very simple.
Extend your hand to someone.
 Open a door.
 Pick up a tab.
 Drive someone to the airport.
 Mow a lawn.
 Pick up medication for someone who cannot get out.
 Say hello to someone who might otherwise be overlooked.
Small things, perhaps. But this is often how the Kingdom quietly appears in the world. It is how we begin to live the way of the true King.
And in the end, we discover something simple and freeing:
Jesus is enough
